_comment: The writing queue, in publication order. The scheduled writing run takes the first entries with status 'pending', writes them, and flips them to 'written'. Dates are assigned at write time by tools/next_slots.py so the schedule stays correct however far behind or ahead it gets.

posts.title: The Great Gods of Samothrace
posts.angle: An initiation open to anyone, on a remote island, whose gods we cannot even reliably name. Philip II met Olympias there. The Nike of Samothrace came from the sanctuary.

posts.title: The Bacchanalia Affair of 186 BCE
posts.angle: Livy's lurid account versus the surviving bronze decree. The Senate legislated against organisation, not debauchery. Cross-link to the pillar and to the Villa of the Mysteries.

posts.title: Isis in Rome: The Goddess Who Travelled
posts.angle: Repeatedly banned by the Republic, embraced by emperors. Apuleius Book 11 as the only initiation narrative. Why an Egyptian goddess out-competed local ones.

posts.title: The Seven Grades of Mithraism
posts.angle: Raven to Father, each tied to a planet. The Ostia mosaic and the Santa Prisca inscriptions. What a promotion ladder implies about a teaching syllabus we have lost entirely.

posts.title: Binding Spells and the Ancient Courtroom
posts.angle: Judicial curse tablets ask for one thing above all: that the opponent be unable to speak. What that reveals about how Greek and Roman trials were actually won.

posts.title: The Evil Eye in the Ancient World
posts.angle: Phallic amulets on doorways, the fascinum worn by children, Pliny on spitting. An anxiety so widespread it shaped domestic architecture.

posts.title: Necromancy in Greece and Rome
posts.angle: From Odysseus at the pit to the recipes in the magical papyri. Legal, illegal, and imperial — emperors consulted the dead and then banned others from doing it.

posts.title: Magical Gems: The Other Half of Ancient Medicine
posts.angle: Thousands of carved gemstones prescribing themselves for stomach pain, childbirth and eye disease, cut with gods and unpronounceable words. Physicians and gem-cutters treated the same complaints and nobody thought that strange. Links to the magical papyri and the curse tablets. Deliberately NOT about envy or the evil eye, which the evil-eye post already covers.

posts.title: The Two Thousand Books Augustus Burned
posts.angle: 12 BCE: the pontifex maximus collects and destroys every unauthorised prophetic book in Rome, keeps the licensed one, edits it, and moves it next to his own house.

posts.title: The Liber Linteus: A Book That Survived as Bandages
posts.angle: The longest surviving Etruscan text reached us wrapped around an Egyptian mummy. A ritual calendar we can read aloud and cannot understand.

posts.title: Why We Still Cannot Read Etruscan
posts.angle: Not a script problem — a language problem. No relatives, no bilinguals of length, and a surviving corpus that is almost entirely gravestones.

posts.title: The Emperor Who Wrote Twenty Books on the Etruscans
posts.angle: Claudius had native speakers, a practising priesthood, state resources, twenty books of research and an endowed annual reading at Alexandria. Every word is gone, and nobody burned it. NOTE: retitled at write time - Suetonius records the Tyrrhenica but mentions no dictionary, and no ancient source does.

posts.title: Delphi: What the Pythia Actually Did
posts.angle: Strip the Victorian imagery. A woman on a tripod, answering yes-or-no questions from states about colonies and wars, with a queue and a fee structure.

posts.title: The Gases Under Delphi
posts.angle: Plutarch describes a sweet-smelling vapour; geologists found intersecting faults and traces of ethylene. Companion piece to the kykeon post — same argument, same honest verdict.

posts.title: Dream Incubation at Epidaurus
posts.angle: Sleep in the sanctuary and the god operates on you in a dream. The inscribed cure testimonies are the strangest medical records to survive antiquity.

posts.title: Reading Lightning: The Etruscan Fulgural Doctrine
posts.angle: Sixteen regions of sky, each with an owner, and a legal procedure for burying a lightning strike. Direct sequel to the Piacenza Liver.

posts.title: The Buried Books of Numa Pompilius
posts.angle: 181 BCE, the Janiculum: farmers dig up two stone chests, one holding Numa's bones, the other his writings. The Senate lets the bones stay buried and burns the books as a threat to state religion. Direct companion to the Augustus post: two burnings for opposite stated reasons. Links to books-augustus-burned and sibylline-books-rome.

posts.title: The Chickens That Sank a Roman Fleet
posts.angle: 249 BCE: a consul asks the sacred chickens for the auspices before Drepana, they refuse to eat, he throws them overboard and loses the fleet. What Roman augury actually was as a technical civic office, distinct from Etruscan haruspicy. Links to etruscan-lightning-doctrine, delphi-pythia and piacenza-liver-etruscan.

posts.title: Cybele's Blood Bath: The Roman Taurobolium
posts.angle: 204 BCE: Rome ships in a black stone on Sibylline orders and calls it the Mother of the Gods, while self-castrated Galli parade in the streets. The same Senate crushed the Bacchanalia eighteen years later. Links to cult-of-isis-rome, bacchanalia-186-bce and mithraism-seven-grades.

posts.title: The Sacred Law of Andania
posts.angle: A 92 BCE inscription of 194 lines regulates the mysteries of Andania in more procedural detail than any Greek mystery cult except Eleusis: seating, dress, fines. Revived by a hierophant named Mnasistratos for reasons the text never explains. Links to eleusinian-mysteries-telesterion and samothrace-great-gods.

posts.title: The Cabeirion: Thebes's Other Mystery Cult
posts.angle: A sanctuary near Thebes where initiates left cups painted with grotesque parodies of the Trojan War, mocking the heroic tradition Thebes claimed descent from. Herodotus calls the rites unspeakable and leaves it there. A deliberately different Great Gods cult from Samothrace. Links to samothrace-great-gods and villa-of-the-mysteries-frescoes.

posts.title: 396 CE: The Night the Mysteries Ended
posts.angle: Alaric's Goths burn the sanctuary at Eleusis months after Theodosius had already outlawed the rites. The best witness, Eunapius, had been initiated by the last legitimate hierophant himself. Direct sequel to the Eleusinian Mysteries post. Links to eleusinian-mysteries-telesterion and eleusinian-kykeon-psychedelic.

posts.title: The Novelist Who Was Tried for Witchcraft
posts.angle: 158 CE, Sabratha: Apuleius stands trial for using magic to seduce a rich widow and defends himself by giving the court a seminar on what real magic looks like. The Apologia is the only complete ancient magic-trial defence to survive. Links to greek-magical-papyri and cult-of-isis-rome.

posts.title: Curse the Charioteer: Magic at the Circus
posts.angle: More than fifty lead tablets from Carthage and Hadrumetum name specific horses and drivers by team colour, calling on demons to break their legs before the race starts, some sharing identical magical formulas. Links to ancient-curse-tablets, ancient-binding-spells-law and evil-eye-ancient-world.

posts.title: The Doll in the Jar: A Love Spell from Egypt
posts.angle: A clay figurine of a bound, kneeling woman, pierced with thirteen needles, found with the lead tablet recipe it was built to follow almost exactly. A fourth-century magician working from a cookbook. Links to greek-magical-papyri and ancient-curse-tablets.

posts.title: The Palladium: Rome's Locked-Room Talisman
posts.angle: A wooden statue only the Vestals and the pontifex maximus could see, sealed in an inner room, said to have come from Troy with Aeneas. A fire in 241 BCE forced Metellus to go in and grab it anyway, and the sources disagree what it cost him. Links to sibylline-books-rome and damnatio-memoriae.

posts.title: The Etruscan Books of the Underworld
posts.angle: The third branch of Etruscan sacred literature: instructions for turning a soul immortal through specific blood sacrifices, quoted only by a hostile Christian polemicist centuries after Etruscan had died as a spoken language. Sequel to the lightning and liver posts. Links to etruscan-lightning-doctrine, piacenza-liver-etruscan and liber-linteus.

posts.title: Pergamon: The Library Built to Beat Alexandria
posts.angle: A royal library built to outdo Alexandria, allegedly starved of papyrus by an Egyptian export ban, which is the origin story told for parchment. Plutarch says Antony later gave the whole collection to Cleopatra, a claim every modern historian who repeats it also flags as unverifiable. Links to library-of-alexandria-what-was-lost and claudius-etruscan-history.

posts.title: The Well That Answered in Oak
posts.angle: At Praeneste the future came out of a well on strips of oak drawn by a child, and in 241 BCE a consul was legally forbidden to consult it. Cicero says only ordinary people ever trusted it, the same century the state trusted the augurs implicitly. Links to delphi-pythia and piacenza-liver-etruscan.

posts.title: Dodona: The Oracle That Answered Everybody
posts.angle: More than four thousand lead strips from Zeus's oldest oracle, most asking not about war or colonies but whose baby a wife is carrying, or whether to take up sheep-farming. Delphi answered states; Dodona answered everybody. Links to delphi-pythia and dream-incubation-asclepius.

posts.title: The Cave They Found Under Virgil's Directions
posts.angle: In 1932 an archaeologist tunnelled into a hillside above Naples and found a 131-metre trapezoidal gallery that matches Virgil's description of the Sibyl's cave closely enough to unnerve people, and still can't be proven to be the actual site. Links to delphi-pythia and sibylline-books-rome.

posts.title: The Oracle That Took Your Smile Away
posts.angle: Consultants at Lebadeia climbed feet-first into a hole in the ground and came out, by multiple accounts, unable to laugh for weeks. Pausanias underwent it himself and wrote up the procedure. Links to dream-incubation-asclepius and oracle-of-the-dead-ephyra.

posts.title: The Rulebook of a Bacchic Club in Athens
posts.angle: A 178 CE inscription of 163 lines from a Dionysiac society in Athens sets out its meeting nights, membership fees, entrance rites, wine allowance and fines for starting fights, in the flat prose of club minutes. It is the fullest picture we have of how a private mystery association actually ran day to day, and it reads more like a dining club than a secret cult. Links to bacchanalia-186-bce and villa-of-the-mysteries-frescoes.

posts.title: Despoina: The Goddess Whose Name Was Secret
posts.angle: At Lykosoura in Arcadia the central figure of the mysteries was called only Despoina, 'the Mistress', because Pausanias says her true name could not be told to the uninitiated. A colossal marble group by Damophon and a stone veil carved with tiny animal-headed dancers are nearly all that survives of the rite. Scholars still argue whether the cult is genuinely archaic Arcadian or a Hellenistic revival dressed as ancient. Links to andania-mysteries-inscription and samothrace-great-gods.

posts.title: The Only Picture of the Eleusinian Procession
posts.angle: A painted clay plaque dedicated at Eleusis around 370 BCE by a woman named Ninnion is the one surviving image that seems to show the Mysteries in progress: torches, myrtle crowns, a seated Demeter, worshippers filing in. Almost every figure is disputed, including whether the scene shows one visit to the sanctuary or two. Links to eleusinian-mysteries-telesterion and eleusinian-kykeon-psychedelic.

posts.title: The Bronze Hands of a God Rome Kept Expelling
posts.angle: Dozens of bronze right hands survive, raised in blessing and covered in symbols: pine cones, snakes, a lizard, a mother nursing a child. They were made for the cult of Sabazios. In 139 BCE a praetor expelled his worshippers from Rome, in a report that also, confusingly, mentions Jews. Whether Sabazios was Phrygian, Thracian, or a hellenised form of Yahweh is still argued. Links to cult-of-cybele-taurobolium and bacchanalia-186-bce.

posts.title: Claros: The Oracle You Consulted at Night
posts.angle: At Klaros near Colophon a priest went down at night into a vaulted underground room, drank from a hidden spring, and gave Apollo's answers in verse, reportedly without being told the questions first. Hundreds of inscriptions record city delegations, and one plague oracle of the 160s CE was copied onto walls from Roman Britain to Syria. How the verses were actually produced is unresolved. Links to delphi-pythia and delphi-gases-hypothesis.

posts.title: Didyma: The Oracle Run by One Family
posts.angle: The oracle at Didyma near Miletus was staffed for centuries by a single clan, the Branchidae, who handed the temple treasure to Persia and then disappeared, possibly massacred by Alexander in reprisal generations later. A prophetess touched a spring and answered; the enormous temple built to house her was never finished. The sources disagree on nearly every detail of the method and the family's end. Links to delphi-pythia and library-pergamon.

posts.title: The Oracles You Worked With Five Knucklebones
posts.angle: Across southern Anatolia stood tall inscribed pillars listing fifty-six numbered replies, each keyed to a single throw of five knucklebones and credited to a named god. You threw, found your verse, and left. It is public divination with the priest removed entirely, and scholars disagree on whether that made it a cheaper cousin of the manned oracles or something people trusted more. Links to delphi-pythia and roman-augury-sacred-chickens.

posts.title: The Fortune-Telling Book of Roman Egypt
posts.angle: The Sortes Astrampsychi is a working fortune-teller's manual preserved on papyrus: ninety-two set questions, an arithmetic trick to select your answer, and ten graded replies for each. 'Will I be sold?' 'Will I get my wages?' It was later Christianised by swapping pagan gods for saints and apostles. How the randomisation really worked, and whether a paid specialist operated it, is still argued. Links to greek-magical-papyri and sibylline-books-rome.

posts.title: The Cursed Spring Under a Roman Garage
posts.angle: A 1999 rescue dig beneath a car park in northern Rome found the sacred spring of Anna Perenna intact, with sealed lead cylinders holding wax and organic figurines, coins, lamps and inscribed curses spanning the first to the sixth century CE. It is the largest sealed deposit of working magic ever excavated. The identity of the figurines and the date of the latest tablets are contested. Links to ancient-curse-tablets and love-spell-doll-louvre.

posts.title: The Getty Hexameters: A Spell Written in Verse
posts.angle: A folded lead sheet from Selinunte, around 400 BCE, carries protective hexameter verses that also appear on amulets across the Greek world and overlap with Orphic material. It surfaced through the antiquities trade with no recorded findspot, and scholars split on whether it is a magical text, a mystery-cult liturgy, or genuinely both at once. Links to orphic-gold-tablets and greek-magical-papyri.

posts.title: The Stones That Confessed a Sin in Public
posts.angle: About a hundred and fifty carved stelai from rural Lydia and Phrygia, mostly second and third century CE, record people announcing publicly that a god had struck them ill for a named offence and that they have now made amends, sometimes with a relief of the afflicted eye or leg. Scholars argue over whether 'confession' is the right word, or whether these mainly advertise the temple's power to punish. Links to evil-eye-ancient-world and ancient-binding-spells-law.

posts.title: Apollonius of Tyana: Sage or Sorcerer
posts.angle: A first-century wandering philosopher credited with cures, foreknowledge, talismans that kept plague and vermin out of cities, and an escape from Domitian's court by vanishing in mid-trial. Nearly all of it comes from one admiring biography written more than a century later for an empress. Later pagans set him against Christ; Christian writers filed him under magic. Links to apuleius-trial-magic and ancient-necromancy.

posts.title: The Astrologers Rome Kept Throwing Out
posts.angle: Rome expelled astrologers from the city at least a dozen times between 139 BCE and the third century CE, frequently under the same emperors who kept personal astrologers and quietly asked them when they would die. The 16 CE expulsion followed the show trial of Libo Drusus. Historians disagree on whether the bans were ever enforced or were largely for show. Links to books-augustus-burned and ancient-necromancy.

posts.title: The Yearly Record Rome Kept, Then Lost
posts.angle: Each year the pontifex maximus posted a whitened board listing grain prices, eclipses, prodigies and magistrates, and the whole run was supposedly collected into eighty books around 120 BCE and then lost. Cato sneered that it recorded how often corn was dear. Bruce Frier argued the eighty-book edition never existed in the form later writers describe. Links to books-augustus-burned and claudius-etruscan-history.

posts.title: Tages: The Child Ploughed Out of a Field
posts.angle: Etruscan religion had an origin story of its own: a ploughman near Tarquinia turned up a furrow, a child with the face of an old man climbed out, dictated the rules for reading livers and lightning to the crowd that gathered, and died the same day. Cicero reports it with a straight face and then takes it apart. The myth sits awkwardly against the discipline's real, partly Near Eastern roots. Links to piacenza-liver-etruscan and numas-buried-books.

posts.title: The Book That Survived Its Own Funeral Pyre
posts.angle: A carbonised roll found in 1962 on a tomb's pyre debris at Derveni near Thessaloniki, Europe's oldest surviving book, is a line-by-line allegorical commentary on an Orphic theogony in which Zeus swallows a phallus. Nobody agrees who wrote it (Euthyphron, Diagoras, Prodicus and Stesimbrotus all have champions) or why it was burned with the dead. Links to orphic-gold-tablets and ancient-mystery-cults-guide.

posts.title: What the Priest Told Alexander at Siwa
posts.angle: In 331 BCE Alexander crossed the Libyan desert to consult Ammon at Siwa and came out, by his own account, saying only that he had heard what he wished. Arrian, Diodorus, Plutarch and Curtius disagree about what was said, and Plutarch's story of a priest's Greek slip ('paidion' for 'pai Dios') is a pun nobody can confirm. Links to dodona-oracle-lead-tablets and didyma-oracle.

posts.title: The Word Square Scratched on a Pompeii Column
posts.angle: SATOR AREPO TENET OPERA ROTAS was scratched into a column of Pompeii's Large Palaestra before 79 CE, and later turns up on Christian amulets from Egypt to Ethiopia. The 1926 PATERNOSTER anagram made it a Christian cryptogram, which the Pompeii find makes awkward; Fishwick, Moeller (a Mithraic reading) and Sheldon disagree, and AREPO still means nothing. Links to greek-magical-gems and greek-magical-papyri.

posts.title: The Jar Buried Near Nag Hammadi
posts.angle: Thirteen leather-bound codices dug up in Upper Egypt in 1945, the famous version of their discovery involving a blood feud and a mother burning pages for kindling. Mark Goodacre has shown how much of that story rests on one informant, and Lundhaug and Jenott argue the books were copied and read by Pachomian monks, not hidden by persecuted heretics. Links to library-of-alexandria-what-was-lost and books-augustus-burned.

posts.title: The Man in the Bona Dea's House
posts.angle: In December 62 BCE Publius Clodius was caught disguised as a woman at the Bona Dea's night rite in Caesar's own house, a rite no man could witness. Cicero's letters give the scandal in real time; what the women actually did inside is preserved mainly as Juvenal's satire and Plutarch's guesswork. Links to villa-of-the-mysteries-frescoes and bacchanalia-186-bce.

posts.title: Glykon, the Snake God with a Human Face
posts.angle: Lucian says Alexander of Abonoteichus faked a talking snake god from a tame python and a linen mask and fleeced half of Asia Minor. Lucian hated him. But coins from Abonoteichus, a marble Glykon from Tomis and inscriptions as far as the Danube show the cult was real and lasted a century after its founder. Links to claros-oracle and dream-incubation-asclepius.

posts.title: The Vestals Rome Buried Alive
posts.angle: A Vestal convicted of unchastity was walled into an underground chamber at the Colline Gate with a lamp, bread and water, so that no one had technically killed her. Pliny watched the case of Cornelia under Domitian and thought she was innocent. Scholars disagree whether these trials were about sex at all, or about crisis: they cluster after disasters like Cannae. Links to palladium-rome and sibylline-books-rome.

posts.title: The Thesmophoria and the Pit of Rotting Pigs
posts.angle: Athenian women camped on the Pnyx for three days each autumn, men barred, and hauled up the decayed remains of piglets thrown into pits months earlier to mix into the seed corn. Almost all of that comes from one scholion on Lucian, of uncertain date. Aristophanes made a comedy of men trying to see inside. Links to eleusinian-mysteries-telesterion and eleusinian-kykeon-psychedelic.

posts.title: The Chaldean Oracles: Verses from the Gods
posts.angle: A second-century collection of hexameter oracles, supposedly delivered by the gods to Julian the Chaldean and his son Julian the Theurgist, who also claimed to have made rain for Marcus Aurelius' army. The book survives only as fragments quoted by Neoplatonists who treated it as scripture. Lewy, Majercik and Johnston disagree on what theurgy actually involved. Links to claros-oracle and greek-magical-papyri.

posts.title: Hippasus and the Secret the Pythagoreans Drowned
posts.angle: The story goes that Hippasus of Metapontum was drowned at sea, by the gods or by his brethren, for revealing the irrational numbers. The sources are late, contradict each other about which secret it was, and Burkert and Zhmud both doubt the irrationals were the issue at all. Links to numas-buried-books and orphic-gold-tablets.

posts.title: Atargatis and the Temple at Hierapolis
posts.angle: Lucian's 'On the Syrian Goddess' describes Atargatis' temple at Hierapolis: sacred fish, a man who climbed a giant phallus twice a year and stayed up seven days, and young men who castrated themselves in the street during the festival. Whether Lucian wrote it, and whether its narrator is a parody of Herodotus, is still argued (Lightfoot 2003). Links to cult-of-cybele-taurobolium and cult-of-isis-rome.

posts.title: The King of the Wood at Nemi
posts.angle: The priest of Diana at Nemi was a runaway slave who held office until another killed him, so he walked the grove armed. Frazer built The Golden Bough on that one custom; C. M. C. Green's study of the sanctuary and its votive deposits argues Frazer misread almost all of it. Links to sortes-praeneste and dream-incubation-asclepius.

posts.title: The Black Stone in the Forum
posts.angle: A patch of black marble paving in the Roman Forum covered a shrine that Romans already half-remembered as Romulus' tomb, and beneath it the oldest Latin inscription in Rome, a curse on whoever disturbs the place, mentioning a 'king'. Festus and Dionysius disagree on whose grave it was; Coarelli and Cornell disagree on what the shrine was. The Romans buried it on purpose. Links to annales-maximi and numas-buried-books.

posts.title: The Sibyl Who Wasn't Rome's
posts.angle: Twelve books of Greek hexameter prophecy in the Sibyl's voice, written by Jewish and then Christian authors over several centuries and quoted by Lactantius and Augustine as pagan witness to Christ. Dating and authorship of almost every book is contested (Collins 1983, Buitenwerf 2003, Lightfoot 2007). Not the lost Roman books, which is the point. Links to sibylline-books-rome and cumaean-sibyl-cave.

posts.title: The Soldiers' God from Doliche
posts.angle: A Syrian storm god standing on a bull, carried by the Roman army from a hilltop in Commagene to Hadrian's Wall and the Aventine, then gone almost overnight in the mid-third century, probably after Shapur I sacked Doliche. No ancient writer describes the cult; it is known only from inscriptions and the German excavations at Dülük Baba Tepesi. Whether it was a mystery cult at all is argued (Speidel 1978, Collar 2013). Links to mithraism-seven-grades and sabazios-hands.

posts.title: The Man Driven Out of the City
posts.angle: At the Thargelia, Ionian cities chose an ugly or worthless man, fed him, beat him with fig branches and drove him out to carry the city's pollution with him. Hipponax's fragments are the earliest evidence; the late lexicographers and Tzetzes say he was burned or thrown from a cliff. Bremmer (1983) and Hughes (1991) doubt anyone was killed. Links to thesmophoria and vestal-virgins-buried-alive.

posts.title: The Library Vesuvius Kept
posts.angle: The only library to survive from the classical world was found in 1752 as lumps of charcoal in a villa at Herculaneum, mostly the Epicurean Philodemus; generations of attempts to unroll them destroyed many, and since 2023 X-ray tomography has begun reading closed ones. The open question is whether the unexcavated lower floors hold a Latin library. Sider (2005) and Gigante on Philodemus; the Vesuvius Challenge results. Links to library-of-alexandria-what-was-lost and library-pergamon.

posts.title: The Dream Interpreter of Daldis
posts.angle: Artemidorus' second-century Oneirocritica is the only ancient dream-interpretation manual to survive whole, built from dreams he collected in markets across the Greek world, and it is frank about sex, money and slavery in a way almost no other ancient text is. Foucault read it as evidence for ancient sexual ethics; Price (1986), Harris-McCoy (2012) and Thonemann (2020) dispute what it can tell us. Links to dream-incubation-asclepius and sortes-astrampsychi.

posts.title: The Letter in the Back of a Book at Mar Saba
posts.angle: In 1958 Morton Smith photographed a letter of Clement of Alexandria copied into the endpapers of a printed book at the monastery of Mar Saba, quoting a 'more spiritual' gospel of Mark kept secret for initiates. The manuscript was later removed and is now lost; only photographs survive. Forgery or genuine is still unresolved (Smith 1973, Carlson 2005, Brown 2005, Jeffery 2007). Links to nag-hammadi-library and eleusinian-mysteries-telesterion.

posts.title: The Hymn the Priests Couldn't Understand
posts.angle: The minutes of the Arval Brethren, carved in stone at their grove outside Rome, record that in 218 CE the priests danced behind closed doors and sang a hymn reading from booklets, because its Latin was so old they could no longer understand it. Scholars still argue what 'enos Lases iuvate' and the rest mean, and how old the hymn really is (Scheid 1990, Beard, North and Price 1998). Links to annales-maximi and roman-augury-sacred-chickens.

posts.title: The Altar on Mount Lykaion
posts.angle: Plato and Pausanias both hint that the secret sacrifice to Zeus on Mount Lykaion in Arcadia involved human flesh and turned whoever ate it into a wolf; Pausanias refuses to describe it. The ash altar excavated since 2004 has produced animal bones, and in 2016 a teenage burial that was reported worldwide as a human sacrifice. Hughes (1991) and Burkert (Homo Necans) read the literary evidence very differently. Links to lykosoura-despoina and vestal-virgins-buried-alive.

posts.title: Hermes Thrice-Great and the Dating That Broke Him
posts.angle: Renaissance readers took the Greek treatises attributed to Hermes Trismegistus as the wisdom of an Egyptian older than Moses, until Isaac Casaubon showed in 1614 that they were written in the Roman period. The swing back since Fowden (1986) is that their Egyptian roots are real after all; Copenhaver (1992) and Bull (2018) weigh how far. Nag Hammadi Codex VI added Hermetic texts no one knew. Links to nag-hammadi-library and greek-magical-papyri.

posts.title: The Day They Took an Axe to Serapis
posts.angle: In 391 a Christian crowd under Bishop Theophilus stormed the Serapeum and a soldier struck the colossal statue of Serapis, whose fall was supposed to end the world. Rufinus and Eunapius tell it from opposite sides; whether any books were still there is the question tied to the Library of Alexandria myth. McKenzie, Gibson and Reyes (JRS 2004) reconstructed the site from excavation. Links to library-of-alexandria-what-was-lost and sack-of-eleusis-396.

posts.title: Opening Virgil to Find Your Fate
posts.angle: The Historia Augusta says Hadrian learned he would be emperor by opening Virgil at random, and the practice ran on into Charles I's reign. But the Historia Augusta is the most unreliable source in Latin, and Syme showed much of it is invented; the solid evidence for book-divination comes from Christian sortes and gospel lot books (Klingshirn 2002, Luijendijk and Klingshirn 2019). Links to sortes-praeneste and sortes-astrampsychi.
